newsitem.title: USA: U.S. elections could set tune for Wall Street.
newsitem.headline: U.S. elections could set tune for Wall Street.

text.p: The political race is in the home stretch and Wall Street is on the sidelines awaiting the election's outcome that could decide whether the six-year-old bull market gets to celebrate another birthday.

The recent batch of economic data have put to rest inflation fears, and with the economy slowing to a comfortable pace, the market is no longer worried that the Federal Reserve will raise interest rates any time soon.
The big unknown, however, is Tuesday's election and the impact it will have on the world's biggest economy.
President Clinton is ahead in opinion polls and the likelihood is that he will win another term, defeating Republican challenger Bob Dole, but the wild card is the House and Senate.
Wall Street has done exceptionally well under Clinton.
The Democratic president has been able to project himself as pro-business and his administration has not promoted legislation that has been viewed as anti-business.
Clinton also has been riding a perfect wave, analysts say, with inflation the lowest in 30 years, the labour market the strongest in seven years and the Dow Jones industrial average soaring.
So far this year, the Dow has set 31 record highs and is up nearly 18 percent from January's level after soaring 34 percent in 1995.
On Friday, the Dow closed 7.45 points lower at 6,021.93 and for the week, it was up 14.91 points.
When Clinton took office, long-term interest rates were above 7 percent, and now they are down to 6.65 percent, their lowest levels in nearly 7 months.

Also helping his re-election chances is that financial markets have reached a comfort level with Clinton who has gotten over the reputation that he acquired early in his term of being a market spoiler instead of a market maker.
What could disrupt the market is a shift of power in the House and Senate from the Republicans to the Democrats.
Although the market has been soaring since Oct. 11, 1990, stocks have taken their biggest leap since shortly after the Republicans won control of Congress in the November elections of 1994.
Stocks would react negatively to a Democratic sweep of both houses, sparking a short-term sell-off of several hundred points in the Dow index, and a jump in long-term interest rates, analysts said.

"The market is hoping for the status-quo but a Democratic sweep of Congress would be a sure-fire reason to expect a short-term drop in the stock market," said Michael Metz, chief investment strategist, at Oppenheimer & Co.
Wall Street, which views the Democrats as a tax-and-spend party, would worry about the approaches that the Democrats take to the nation's economic and trade policy.
The Republicans, on the other hand, are traditionally more trusted than Democrats to avoid high-spending that scares the financial markets.
Hugh Johnson, chief investment officer at First Albany Corp. said the Dow index could fall by 5 percent or 300 points if Democrats recaptured Congress.

"Under a Democratically controlled Congress, the perception is likely to take hold that deficit reductions will be put on back burners, and the Democrats and Clinton will not have the 'stuff' to cut spending, particularly entitlements, such as Social Security, Medicare and Medicaid," Johnson said.
He said the stock market was already delicately balanced after its run-up and the election could tip the scale and bring a sharp correction.
"Both bonds and stocks are on thin ice and it takes a real roll of the dice to be a player at these high levels with this election coming up," Johnson said.

The current House party breakdown is 235-197, with one independent who usually votes with the Democrats, and two vacancies. Democrats need to pick up 19 seats to control the House. Republicans hold the Senate 53-47. All 435 House seats, and 34 Senate seats, are up for election.

Analysts believe that a victory by Dole also would not play well to the market. Dole's across-the-board tax cut of 15 percent, which carries a price tag of $548 billion, is very ambitious and would likely spark an unsettling jump in interest rates.
"If Dole squeezes in, the markets' one hour reaction would be bullish initially but there eventually would be a drop in stocks and bonds," Metz said.
At least one expert dismissed the impact of the political contest on the economy.

Louis Rukeyser, editor of the Wall Street investment letter says the economy was still in great shape and corporate America was very competitive after years of restructuring and investors should sit back and not worry about what the politicians will do to the economy.
"The country is a heck of a lot stronger than its politicians," he said. "Happily, these wet-finger-in-the-wind leaders are far less crucial to our economy's prospects than they so grandly pretend."

For the week, the Standard & Poor's composite index of 500 stocks rose 2.85 points to 703.77; the Nasdaq composite index slipped 0.82 to 1,221.78; the American Stock Exchange index rose 2.79 to 572.58; and the NYSE composite index of all listed common stocks edged up 0.42 to 373.68.
